# Describing Data

In Term 1, you used R to describe data and conducted some basic statistical testing. Over the next three sessions, we will go back over some of this ground, but more slowly and with a clear purpose: to understand what the numbers mean, how sure we can be about them, and when a difference between groups is real. We will use one question throughout: **who breathes the most polluted air in London?** This week, we will set up a *tidy* workflow in R and use it to describe our data. This session and the next link to the first statistics worksheet.

The code is a means to an end. What matters is that you understand what each step does and why, so that you can tell whether a result makes sense. Throughout these sessions, we will therefore regularly ask you to **predict** a result before you run the code, and then **check** whether you were right.

::: {.callout-important}
## Before the session
Make sure **R** and **RStudio** are working on your laptop. You installed both in Term 1; if you run into problems, you can use [Desktop@UCL Anywhere](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/isd/services/computers/remote-access/desktopucl-anywhere) instead. Then run the following once in the RStudio console to install the `tidyverse`:

```r
install.packages('tidyverse')
```
:::

## Air pollution in London
**Nitrogen dioxide** (NO~2~) mostly comes from road traffic, and long-term exposure is linked to asthma and other respiratory diseases. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that the annual mean should not exceed **10 µg/m³**, with *interim targets* of 40, 30 and 20 µg/m³ for places that are still far above this guideline. The UK legal limit is **40 µg/m³**. Fine particulate matter (PM~2.5~) comes from traffic, wood burning and many other sources, and has a WHO guideline of **5 µg/m³**.

Air pollution is a physical phenomenon, but who is exposed to it is a social question. Researchers refer to this as **environmental justice**: are poorer neighbourhoods exposed to more pollution than richer ones? Over the next three sessions, we will describe, estimate and test exactly that.

## The data
We will be using a dataset that contains one row for each of London's 4,994 Lower Super Output Areas (LSOAs): small statistical areas with, on average, about 1,500 residents. For each LSOA, the dataset contains the following variables:

| Column | Description |
| :----- | :---------- |
| `lsoa_code`, `lsoa_name` | LSOA code and name (2021) |
| `borough`, `inner_outer` | London borough, and whether it is in Inner or Outer London |
| `population` | Residents (mid-2022) |
| `no2`, `pm25` | Modelled annual mean NO~2~ and PM~2.5~, 2022 (µg/m³), averaged over the LSOA |
| `imd_score`, `imd_decile` | Index of Multiple Deprivation 2025: score, and decile within England (1 = most deprived 10%) |
| `income_score` | Share of residents who are income-deprived (0 to 1) |

The NO~2~ and PM~2.5~ values are **averages over whole LSOAs**. No LSOA as a whole is above the UK legal limit, but many roadside locations within them are.

::: {.callout-note}
## Data sources
Greater London Authority, *London Atmospheric Emissions Inventory (LAEI) 2022*, 20 m concentration grids, averaged per LSOA. Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government, *English Indices of Deprivation 2025*. LSOA boundaries: Office for National Statistics. All under the Open Government Licence v3.0.
:::

## A tidy workflow
In Term 1, you worked with **base R**: functions such as `read.csv()` and `tapply()`, and the `$` operator. In these sessions, we will switch to the `tidyverse`: a collection of packages that share a common way of working. You take a dataset and pass it through a series of small steps using the pipe, `|>`, which you can read as *"and then"*. This is also how R is used in most Year 2 methods modules.

Let us start by loading the `tidyverse` and reading in the data. The `glimpse()` function gives us a first look at the dataset: the number of rows and columns, the type of each column, and the first few values.

```{r}
#| label: 05-load
#| filename: 'R code'
#| message: false
# load the tidyverse
library(tidyverse)

# read the data
lsoa <- read_csv('data/london-lsoa-air-quality.csv')

# a first look: rows, columns, types and first values
glimpse(lsoa)
```

The `tidyverse` is built around a small number of **verbs**, each of which does one thing. The table below lists the most important ones, together with their base R equivalents from Term 1:

| Verb | What it does | Base R from Term 1 |
| :--- | :----------- | :----------------- |
| `select()` | keep some columns | `df[, c('a', 'b')]` |
| `filter()` | keep rows that meet a condition | `df[df$a > 10, ]` |
| `mutate()` | add or change a column | `df$c <- df$a / df$b` |
| `arrange()` | sort rows | `df[order(df$a), ]` |
| `group_by()` + `summarise()` | summarise per group | `tapply(df$a, df$g, mean)` |
| `count()` | count rows per group | `table(df$g)` |

Let us try some of these. Each pipe below starts with the dataset and passes it through one or more verbs:

```{r}
#| label: 05-verbs
#| filename: 'R code'
# the five LSOAs with the highest NO2
lsoa |>
  select(lsoa_name, borough, no2) |>
  arrange(desc(no2)) |>
  head(5)

# how many LSOAs in Inner and Outer London?
lsoa |>
  count(inner_outer)

# LSOAs in Hackney with NO2 above 25
lsoa |>
  filter(borough == 'Hackney', no2 > 25) |>
  nrow()
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise icon=false}
## Try it yourself
Rather than writing new code from scratch, it is often quicker to adapt code that already works. Change the first pipe so that it shows the five LSOAs with the **lowest** PM~2.5~, and the last one so that it counts the LSOAs in a borough of your choice with NO~2~ above 20.
:::

We can use `mutate()` to add new columns. Every LSOA in London is above the WHO guideline of 10 µg/m³, so instead we will flag each LSOA that is above the WHO interim target of 20 µg/m³. We will also divide London's LSOAs into five equally sized groups (**quintiles**) based on income deprivation, from 1 (the least deprived fifth) to 5 (the most deprived fifth). Because we will use both new columns again, we save the result by assigning it back to `lsoa`:

```{r}
#| label: 05-mutate
#| filename: 'R code'
# add two columns
lsoa <- lsoa |>
  mutate(above_20 = no2 > 20,
         income_quintile = ntile(income_score, 5))

# check: about 1,000 LSOAs in each quintile
lsoa |>
  count(income_quintile)
```

::: {.callout-note}
Why do we use income deprivation rather than the overall Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD)? The IMD includes a *Living Environment* domain that partly measures air quality, so comparing NO~2~ with the IMD would partly mean comparing air pollution with itself. Using Income deprivation only avoids this problem.
:::

## Describing a single variable
When we describe a numerical variable, we usually report three things: its **centre**, its **spread** and its **shape**. We can calculate the most common summary statistics in one go with `summarise()`.

::: {.callout-note .exercise icon=false}
## Predict first
A few LSOAs have much higher NO~2~ than the rest (you saw the top five above). Do you expect the mean to be above or below the median? Run the code and check.
:::

```{r}
#| label: 05-describe
#| filename: 'R code'
# centre and spread of NO2
lsoa |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean = mean(no2),
            median = median(no2),
            sd = sd(no2),
            iqr = IQR(no2),
            min = min(no2),
            max = max(no2))
```

- **Centre**: the *mean* is the average, and the *median* is the middle value. If the two differ a lot, the distribution is skewed or contains outliers.
- **Spread**: the *standard deviation* (sd) is roughly the typical distance of a value from the mean, and the *interquartile range* (IQR) is the range covered by the middle 50% of values.
- **Shape**: is the distribution symmetric or skewed, and does it have one peak or more? To see this, we need a plot.

For plotting, we will keep using **base R**, as in Term 1. Note that the `$` operator still works on a dataset loaded with the `tidyverse`:

```{r}
#| label: fig-05-hist
#| fig-cap: Distribution of annual mean NO2 across London LSOAs, 2022.
#| filename: 'R code'
# histogram, with the WHO interim target as a dashed line
hist(lsoa$no2, breaks = 40,
     main = 'NO2 in London LSOAs, 2022',
     xlab = 'Annual mean NO2 (µg/m³)', ylab = 'Number of LSOAs',
     col = 'grey80', border = 'white')
abline(v = 20, lty = 2)
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise icon=false}
## Try it yourself
Proportions are means too. Because `above_20` is either `TRUE` (1) or `FALSE` (0), its mean is the share of LSOAs above the interim target. Try running `mean(lsoa$above_20)`. What does the answer tell you?
:::

### Areas or people?
The mean we calculated treats every LSOA as one unit. However, LSOAs differ in the number of people who live in them, and if we want to say something about *people*, we should count people. A **population-weighted mean** does exactly that:

```{r}
#| label: 05-weighted
#| filename: 'R code'
# average LSOA vs average Londoner
lsoa |>
  summarise(mean_lsoa = mean(no2),
            mean_resident = weighted.mean(no2, population))
```

In this case the two values are very close, but it is always worth asking yourself whether your unit of analysis is the area or the person.

## Describing groups
We can compare groups by combining `group_by()` with `summarise()`, the `tidyverse` equivalent of `tapply()`. Let us compare NO~2~ levels in Inner and Outer London:

```{r}
#| label: 05-group
#| filename: 'R code'
# NO2 in Inner and Outer London
lsoa |>
  group_by(inner_outer) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean = mean(no2),
            median = median(no2),
            sd = sd(no2))
```

A **boxplot** shows the median, the IQR (the box) and any outliers for each group side by side. The formula `no2 ~ inner_outer` can be read as "NO~2~ by Inner or Outer London":

```{r}
#| label: fig-05-box-io
#| fig-cap: NO2 in Inner and Outer London LSOAs.
#| filename: 'R code'
# boxplot by group
boxplot(no2 ~ inner_outer, data = lsoa,
        main = 'NO2 by part of London',
        xlab = '', ylab = 'Annual mean NO2 (µg/m³)')
```

The same approach works for the boroughs. With 33 boroughs, it helps to sort the result, so that we can look at the boroughs with the highest and the lowest levels:

```{r}
#| label: 05-borough
#| filename: 'R code'
# borough summary, sorted by median NO2
borough_no2 <- lsoa |>
  group_by(borough) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            median = median(no2),
            iqr = IQR(no2),
            share_above_20 = mean(above_20)) |>
  arrange(desc(median))

head(borough_no2, 5)
tail(borough_no2, 5)
```

## Pollution and deprivation
Let us now return to our environmental justice question, and look at NO~2~ levels for each income deprivation quintile.

::: {.callout-note .exercise icon=false}
## Predict first
Which quintile do you expect to have the highest NO~2~, and do you expect a steady increase from quintile 1 to quintile 5?
:::

```{r}
#| label: 05-quintile
#| filename: 'R code'
# NO2 by income deprivation quintile
lsoa |>
  group_by(income_quintile) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean = mean(no2),
            median = median(no2),
            sd = sd(no2))
```

And plot the result:

```{r}
#| label: fig-05-box-quintile
#| fig-cap: NO2 by income deprivation quintile (1 = least deprived fifth of London LSOAs).
#| filename: 'R code'
boxplot(no2 ~ income_quintile, data = lsoa,
        main = 'NO2 by income deprivation',
        xlab = 'Income deprivation quintile (1 = least, 5 = most deprived)',
        ylab = 'Annual mean NO2 (µg/m³)')
```

It is worth looking carefully before drawing any conclusions. Is the pattern the same all the way from quintile 1 to quintile 5? Also remember that both deprived areas and polluted areas are more common in Inner London.

::: {.callout-note .exercise icon=false}
## Try it yourself
Repeat the summary **within** Inner and Outer London, using `group_by(inner_outer, income_quintile)`. Before you run it, predict whether the pattern will still hold in both parts of London, and then check.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
Describing is not the same as explaining. A difference between groups tells us *that* exposure is unequal, but not *why*: roads, housing, history and planning all play a part.
:::

## Reporting your results
In a report, an essay or a worksheet, we describe our data in a short paragraph supported by a figure, rather than by copying R output. A good description covers:

- **what** was measured, in which **units**, for which **units of analysis** (LSOAs, people), and **how many**;
- the **centre** and **spread**, with suitable measures (median and IQR if the data are skewed);
- the **shape**, shown in a figure that you refer to;
- how groups **differ**, in numbers and in words, without claiming more than the data show.

Based on this session's results, this could look as follows:

> Across London's `r format(nrow(lsoa), big.mark = ',')` LSOAs, modelled annual mean NO~2~ in 2022 had a median of `r sprintf('%.1f', median(lsoa$no2))` µg/m³ (IQR `r sprintf('%.1f', IQR(lsoa$no2))` µg/m³), ranging from `r min(lsoa$no2)` to `r max(lsoa$no2)` µg/m³. Every LSOA was above the WHO guideline of 10 µg/m³, and `r round(100 * mean(lsoa$above_20))`% were above the interim target of 20 µg/m³. Levels were clearly higher in Inner London (median `r sprintf('%.1f', median(lsoa$no2[lsoa$inner_outer == 'Inner']))` µg/m³) than in Outer London (`r sprintf('%.1f', median(lsoa$no2[lsoa$inner_outer == 'Outer']))` µg/m³).

::: {.callout-note .exercise icon=false}
## Try it yourself
Write a similar paragraph for PM~2.5~.
:::

- [ ] used `select()`, `filter()`, `mutate()`, `arrange()`, `group_by()` + `summarise()` and `count()`;

## Troubleshooting
| Problem | What to try |
| :------ | :---------- |
| `could not find function "read_csv"` | Run `library(tidyverse)` first. If that fails, run `install.packages('tidyverse')`. |
| `'data/london-lsoa-air-quality.csv' does not exist` | Is your project open? Is the file in the `data` folder, with exactly this name? If you downloaded it twice, your browser may have saved it as `london-lsoa-air-quality (1).csv`: rename it. |
| `object 'lsoa' not found` | Run the lines that create it first. Run your script from the top. |
| `object 'income_quintile' not found` | You ran `mutate()` without saving the result. Start the line with `lsoa <-`, as in the code above, and run it again. |
| A plot looks squashed | Make the [Plots]{.ui} pane bigger, or click [Zoom]{.ui}. |
